claims.text: Tribological performance of HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices varies non-monotonically with ambient temperature.
Intermediate temperatures promote formation of adaptive, self-lubricating oxide tribo-layers.
Performance degrades significantly at or above an approximately 600 °C boundary.
Excessive oxidation of refractory elements above the boundary produces brittle phases and loss of mechanical integrity.
CuMoTaWV and CoNiCuFeCr-Nb are examples of HEA coating systems that may be deposited on steel or Ni-based transition-metal matrices.
The initial HEA coating has a nanocrystalline or multiphase microstructure.
The initial HEA coating has high hardness associated with solution strengthening.
The relevant structural mediator is the formation and evolution of a tribo-oxide layer containing oxides such as CuO, MoO3, V2O5, or Ta/W oxides.
A dense oxide tribo-layer at intermediate temperature reduces friction and wear by limiting direct metal-to-metal contact.
Oxidation kinetics accelerate excessively beyond the critical temperature and form thick, brittle, voluminous oxide scales.
The brittle oxide scales fracture under sliding shear stress and generate abrasive debris.
Oxide-scale fracture causes a transition from mild oxidative wear to severe delamination and galling.
Wear rate decreases between room temperature and an optimum near 400 °C, where COF and wear are minimized.
Near 600 °C, wear rate increases sharply and COF rises or fluctuates because the oxide layer becomes unstable, resulting in surface spallation.
At room temperature, the as-deposited coating typically has moderate wear dominated by abrasive and adhesive mechanisms without significant oxide lubrication.
The degradation boundary occurs when oxide formation outpaces tribo-film repair and causes catastrophic failure of the protective layer.
The exact degradation temperature depends on alloy composition and counterface material because oxide-layer stability is composition-dependent.
